passages.P4: Democrat Nate McMurray at a NY-27 debate on Oct. 21, 2020. (Robert Kirkham/Buffalo News)
passages.P8: # Jacob’s charge that McMurray raised taxes on Grand Island is correct
passages.P9: In a rematch between Rep. Chris Jacobs, a Republican, and Democrat Nate McMurray for the 27th Congressional District seat, Jacobs says his opponent has a track record of raising taxes and a desire to do so again.
passages.P10: In a large postcard sent to voters, the Jacobs campaign links McMurray with Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of Queens and says: “Nate McMurray Big Tax, Big Spend: An AOC Progressive Who Will Raise Taxes.”
passages.P11: The mailer claims that “While serving as Town Supervisor, Nate McMurray voted to raise taxes on homeowners.”
passages.P12: We were curious about McMurray’s record on Grand Island, where he served as supervisor for four years, beginning in 2016.
passages.P14: We spoke with McMurray, who confirmed that as a member of the town board on Grand Island, he voted to slightly increase taxes. He also proposed budgets, as supervisor, with slight tax increases, he said.
passages.P15: During all four years of his tenure, the increases remained under the property tax cap, he said. He also said that he was one of five people on the board, where Republicans held the other four seats.
passages.P16: “I had no control to raise taxes myself,” he said.
passages.P17: Taxes increased about $27 in 2018 for a house assessed at $210,600. The tax rate for the general fund, which makes up a large amount of town spending, decreased by 3.1%, but an increase in the sewer district tax led to the increase. The 20% of residents without sewer access generally did not have an increase.
passages.P18: The town’s official meeting minutes of the board session with the budget vote show that McMurray voted in favor of the increase.
passages.P19: McMurray said he sometimes had to fight to keep the increases from getting too high during negotiations with other board members. “I’m one of five, and everybody has their pet thing.”
passages.P20: In the 2019 budget, adopted in late 2018, the tax levy, or the amount raised in taxes, increased by 28% on Grand Island for the sewer system fund, though overall levy increase was 2.63 percent. Rates increased only for people using the sewer system and went down for those who do not. The combined levy for the general and highway funds fell by 4%. McMurray voted in favor of this budget.
passages.P21: The town’s sewer system needed costly repairs, and a prior administration reached a deal with the state Department of Environmental Conservation, McMurray said. It was his administration’s obligation to fund them, he said, a statement supported by a 2017 outside auditor’s report.
passages.P22: The general fund tax rate was lower when he left office than it was during his first year, but that is not true of all of the funds that tax residents.
passages.P23: McMurray said that the mailer makes it seem like he was recklessly raising taxes as supervisor. “It’s acting like we’re willy-nilly raising taxes,” he said. “Sure, there was a moderate increase under the tax cap.”
passages.P24: McMurray has campaigned on his fiscal management of Grand Island, including a claim from 2018, in which he said he was a “small-town supervisor who has kept a balanced budget, who has increased surpluses, who has led us to the highest credit rating our town has ever had.” PolitiFact rated that claim True.

passages.P2: stated on August 8, 2018 in a news conference at the UAW 897 hall in Hamburg. :
passages.P3: **Says he’s a “small-town supervisor who has kept a balanced budget, who has increased surpluses, who has led us to the highest credit rating our town has ever had.”**
passages.P8: # McMurray claims financial victories on Grand Island
passages.P9: As Democrat Nathan McMurray looks for votes in a Republican-leaning congressional district, he points to his record as Grand Island town supervisor the last two and a half years.
passages.P10: On Aug. 8, the day Republican incumbent Chris Collins was arrested on insider trading charges, McMurray held a news conference and prepared his supporters for the attacks he said will come in the race for New York’s 27th Congressional District.
passages.P11: “The cheaters are still going to fight,” McMurray said. “They’re still going to try to cheat. They’re going to try to label me, someone who’s been a small-town supervisor, who has kept a balanced budget, who has increased surpluses, who has led us to the highest credit rating our town has ever had, who is an Eagle Scout, who is a father and a husband and a dad, that I’m some type of radical because I have a D next to my name. When is this game of party affiliation going to end?”
passages.P12: We decided to evaluate the claims he made about his tenure as Grand Island supervisor. He began a four-year term in January 2016.
passages.P14: Local governments must adopt balanced budgets, according to the New York State Comptroller’s Office. Excluding capital projects which are funded by debt not included in balanced budget calculations, the town took in $19.9 million in 2016 and spent $18.6 million, according to the town’s financial statements.
passages.P15: In 2017, the town posted revenues of $20 million and spent $19.1 million.
passages.P16: Deducting spending on capital projects from the town’s financial statements is the most accurate way to evaluate McMurray’s balanced budget claim, said Pam Barton, Grand Island’s accountant.
passages.P18: Is that the same as a surplus?
passages.P19: The generally accepted definition of “surplus” in town government is the amount of money in “unassigned fund balance” in the town’s general fund, Barton said.
passages.P20: For Grand Island, the unassigned fund balance was $5.9 million in 2015, the year before McMurray took office, $6.8 million in 2016 and $6.7 million in 2017. It dropped a bit last year but was still higher than the surplus from the year before he took office.
passages.P22: Grand Island received its highest credit rating since at least 2001 in September 2016, Barton said.
passages.P23: When Barton became town accountant in 2001, the town’s bond rating was A2, she said, four notches below its current rating of Aa1 by Moody’s Investors Service.
passages.P24: The town’s current rating is the second-highest on Moody’s scale. Barton said because of the town’s size and budget, it likely will never reach the highest rating.
passages.P25: Barton said the town has always been rated by Moody’s, and has not received ratings from Standard & Poor’s or Fitch Ratings.
passages.P27: McMurray made three claims about his record of managing Grand Island’s finances.
passages.P28: It’s fair to point out that Grand Island’s strong financial position is the result of years of sound management, not only changes made since McMurray took office in 2016, Barton said.
passages.P29: “He’s been continuing the things that have been in place from before,” the town accountant said.
passages.P30: Still, his claim about keeping a balanced budget is true.

passages.P9: # Election 2015: McMurray wins Grand Island town supervisor race
passages.P13:
Nathan
McMurray won the Town of Grand Island supervisor's race after a canvas of votes
Wednesday.
passages.P14:
The
two-vote lead McMurray held over incumbent Mary Cooke on election night Nov. 3
extended to 14 votes after counting of absentee and affidavit ballots Tuesday
and a canvass of votes Wednesday at the Erie County Board of Elections in
Buffalo.
passages.P15:
McMurray
won 2,768 to 2,754. He led 2,674 to 2,672 on election night.
passages.P16:
"I'm very
excited. But I am also humbled and thankful for the opportunity to serve," said
McMurray Thursday via email from Ireland, where he was at a business
conference. "I want to thank the current supervisor for all of her years of
service and wish her and her family the best. I also want everyone on Grand
Island to know that I recognize that this was a tight election. I will do
everything in my power to not disappoint those who voted for me, and to win
over those who did not. But whether you are a supporter or not, I will do my
best to listen to and represent all of Grand Island in a manner that
strengthens us, binds us closer together, and makes us proud."
passages.P17:
Cooke, who
was seeking a second term as supervisor, said Thursday she was at the Board of
Elections for the counting Wednesday, a process that took three hours.
passages.P18:
"This was
quite an exercise yesterday," Cooke said of the counting process undertaken
Wednesday. "Obviously I'm disappointed in the results and I would have
preferred not to have it be so close that we had to go down there and do that,
but I certainly appreciated the opportunity to see the process in action."
passages.P19:
"I'm
disappointed because I ran to win, but my biggest frustration is the campaign
that was run," Cooke said. "The campaign run against the team I was on was
negative and very personal and filled with half-truths and personal attacks,
and that's in my opinion wrong. And so that's extremely frustrating."
passages.P20:
Cooke
repeated a complaint she made on election night of her opponent's web log,
where McMurray had posted updates frequently during his campaign. Cooke said
that six-and-a-half months of her opponent's blog "vaporized the night of
election night is also extremely suspect to me and makes me wonder what that
was all about."
passages.P21:
"All of
the very vicious attacks of me, other teammates on the ticket and town staff
are gone," she said of votemcmurray.com.
passages.P23:
"It's been an honor and
a privilege to serve and I certainly am disappointed in the election results,
but I also know that life will carry on and I'm looking forward to -- I don't
know exactly what -- looking forward to the future," Cooke said about her
plans. "There's going to be all sorts of opportunities that I haven't been able
to do because of the time crunch, so that's an attraction. But I also have a
lot of interest in the town and will continue to work on the projects that I
did before I was supervisor and have great interest in."

records.title: Attempting something way out of my comfort zone, but I think it ...
records.retrieval_query: What primary records (meeting minutes, ordinances, resolutions, or roll-call votes) document Nate McMurray's votes while serving as Town Supervisor on Grand Island, Nebraska?

passages.P1: Attempting something way out of my comfort zone, but I think it could be beneficial in the long run. I attended a Board Of Governors meeting last night for the Pine Island Ridge Community. Every morning I see roughly 20-30 high school kids wait around this area for the bus. Plus, roughly 10 vehicles parking on the swale and such. It’s early, it’s dark, and of course…it’s hot. At the meeting last night I asked to speak in their open forum and suggested a covered structure of some kind be proposed so the kids wouldn’t have to wait by the road. With power and lighting as well. The area is a basically a green space right now with a few benches with no cover and really isn’t being utilized like it could be in my humble opinion. This used to be a playground. Now, I understand folks don’t like to see anymore concrete structures being erected in this town, but if it’s beneficial to many folks who live in the community and the funds are available without raising HOA fees. Why not think about it? It’s not just high school kids. It’s also middle schoolers, elementary kids, preschoolers, it could be a designated Uber and Lyft pick up/drip off. Then, it could possibly be rented for small events. Maybe add some bbq pits as well? If you live in Pine Island Ridge, I’d love to know if this is a good idea or a complete waste of time and resources. Thoughts, suggestions, ideas?
passages.P9: I agree, at least a gazebo in the park area for them to wait!
passages.P14: Let them make one out of thatch. No concrete required.
passages.P15: I also think it’s less expensive or there is no permit process. There’s something about that. …
passages.P18: The issue is that it’s a natural preserve. Which is why the playground got moved to near the tennis courts.
